passages.t: No one upright left, and waiting for God
passages.happening:
The prophet grieves. He is like someone gathering summer fruit after the harvest, who finds no cluster to eat and no early fig (verse 1). ‘The godly man has perished from the earth; there is no one upright among men’ (verse 2). They lie in wait for blood and hunt each other with nets. The prince and the judge ask for bribes, and the powerful say what they want and the rest join in (verse 3). The best of them is like a briar (verse 4).

Do not rely on a friend or trust a companion, and guard your words even with the one who lies in your arms (verse 5). ‘For a son dishonors his father, a daughter rises against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s enemies are the members of his own household’ (verse 6).

‘But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The opening picture comes from the harvest. After the main picking of grapes and figs, the poor were allowed to glean what was left. The prophet is like a hungry gleaner who finds the vines already stripped: not one upright person is left to find. The early fig, which ripened in late spring before the main crop, was a special treat, and its absence deepens the loss.

The social breakdown fits the same world as chapters 2, 3 and 6: officials and judges for sale, powerful men setting the agenda, and people who have learned to trust no one. The list in verses 5 and 6 moves inward from friend to companion to spouse to children, the whole circle of trust in a household, and shows each ring failing. In a culture built on family loyalty, that was a picture of complete collapse.

Verse 7 is the hinge of the chapter. The prophet does not pretend things are better than they are. He looks to God and waits.
passages.later: The law left the gleanings of the harvest for the poor (Leviticus 19:9-10). Jesus quoted verse 6 when he warned that following him could divide families: ‘A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household’ (Matthew 10:36).
passages.asks: The prophet looked around and found no one he could trust. Ask where you feel that kind of loneliness. And then, with him, ask what it would mean to look to the LORD and wait, trusting that God will hear you.

passages.happening:
Now the city speaks. “Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light” (verse 8). Because she has sinned against him, she must bear the LORD's anger until he pleads her case and brings justice for her. ‘He will bring me into the light; I will see His righteousness’ (verse 9). Her enemy, who mocked her by asking where her God was, will be covered with shame (verse 10).

A day will come for rebuilding her walls and extending her boundary (verse 11). People will come to her from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, from sea to sea and mountain to mountain (verse 12). But the earth will be desolate because of what its people have done (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a kind of liturgy, a series of voices that could be read in worship. Here Zion speaks as a woman who has fallen and answers her gloating enemy, also pictured as a woman. She does not deny her sin. She accepts the LORD's anger as just, and she trusts him to be her advocate in the end.

Many scholars think verses 8 to 20 reflect the later time of exile or return, with a ruined city waiting for its walls to be rebuilt, and some date them to the sixth century BC. Others read them as Micah's own looking ahead to judgment and restoration, in keeping with his warning that Zion would be plowed and his mention of Babylon. Either way, Jews who had lived through Jerusalem's fall read the chapter as a word to them.

The enemy's taunt, where is the LORD your God, is the mockery the psalms also know. The answer is not that Zion was never in the wrong, but that God will bring her into the light.
passages.later: A psalm asks why the nations should say such things of God's people (Psalm 115:2), and Isaiah promised, ‘Arise, shine, for your light has come’ (Isaiah 60:1).
passages.asks: Zion says that though she has fallen she will rise, and she owns her sin while she says it. Ask whether you can admit what you have done and still hope in God's light. And ask whose fall you have been tempted to gloat over.

passages.t: Who is a God like you?
passages.happening:
The prophet prays: ‘Shepherd with Your staff Your people, the flock of Your inheritance’ (verse 14). Let them graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old. God answers that he will show wonders, as when they came out of Egypt (verse 15). The nations will see and be ashamed, and tremble before the LORD (verses 16-17).

The hymn begins, ‘Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance’ (verse 18), who does not hold on to his anger forever, because he delights in loving devotion. He will again have compassion. ‘He will vanquish our iniquities. You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea’ (verse 19). ‘You will show faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from the days of old’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Bashan and Gilead were fertile pastures east of the Jordan, taken by Tiglath-pileser III around 733 or 732 BC. A prayer to graze there again as in the days of old is a prayer for land Micah's generation had seen lost. Shepherd your people with your staff turns the royal picture of 5:4 into a prayer to God himself. The nations licking dust like a snake echo the curse on the serpent in Genesis.

The closing question, who is a God like you, plays on the prophet's own name, Micah, which means who is like the LORD. The book ends by turning his name into a confession. The last verse joins faithfulness and loving devotion, the pair God made known to Moses at Sinai, to Jacob and Abraham, rooting the future in the oldest promises.

In later Jewish practice, verses 18 to 20 became part of Tashlikh, a new year custom of going to flowing water and casting away sins as a sign, and they are read in the synagogue on the Day of Atonement after the book of Jonah.
passages.later: God proclaimed himself to Moses as ‘abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness’ (Exodus 34:6). A psalm says, ‘As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us’ (Psalm 103:12).
passages.hard:
How can God's anger and his delight in mercy both be true, as verses 9 and 18 say?

The chapter holds both without embarrassment. Zion admits that she must bear the LORD's anger because she has sinned, and a few verses later God is praised for not holding on to his anger forever. Some readers find this a contradiction, as if God were changeable or quick-tempered. The Old Testament's own answer, rooted in God's words to Moses at Sinai, is that God's anger is the settled opposition of a good God to evil that harms his people and his world, while his mercy is his deeper purpose, the thing he delights in. Anger in Scripture is real but not final; mercy is the direction in which God's dealings run.

Christian theology later found the meeting point of the two at the cross, where God's judgment on sin and his mercy toward sinners meet in one act. Readers differ on how to describe the relationship between God's wrath and his love, but the chapter refuses to drop either.
passages.asks: The book ends by asking who is a God like this one, who pardons and delights in mercy. Ask what sin you have kept that God has offered to throw into the depths of the sea. And ask what it would mean to believe that he does not stay angry forever.
